chunks: "KCL and KVL are Kirchhoff's two laws, and they're really conservation laws.
KCL, the current law, says the sum of currents entering any node equals the sum leaving, or equivalently, the algebraic sum is zero.
That's conservation of charge: a node is just a junction of wires, so it can't store charge, and whatever comes in has to go out.
If 5 milliamps comes into a node and one branch takes 2 milliamps, the other branches together take 3 milliamps.
KVL, the voltage law, says the sum of the voltages around any closed loop is zero.
That's conservation of energy: voltage is potential, so if I walk around a loop and come back to the same node, my net change in potential has to be zero.
So in a series loop, the source voltage equals the sum of the drops across the resistors.
Together with Ohm's law they let you solve any circuit: KCL at the nodes, KVL around loops. The caveat is they assume a lumped circuit.
At high frequencies, or if a loop links a changing magnetic field, you get induced voltages, which is why ground loops and long scope ground leads pick up noise."
